Friday, 8 pm.
Today at lunch I grabbed Nirmala's new gel pen and wouldn't give it back. When she reached for it I pulled so hard it snapped in two. She went quiet and her eyes got shiny. I said, "It was already broken," which was a lie. My stomach hurt all afternoon.
After school I walked to her gate. I said, "I'm sorry I broke your pen, and I lied. I did it because I was showing off." She didn't say anything for a bit. Then she said, "Okay." I gave her two pens from my own pencil box and helped her stick her diary cover back, which had ripped too.
We played catch after that. Mummy asked why I looked lighter. I don't know.
— Ritu

qa.q: What did Ritu give Nirmala after breaking the pen?
qa.a: Ritu gave Nirmala two pens from Ritu's own pencil box.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during the afternoon after breaking the pen?
qa.a: Ritu felt guilty and uneasy, shown by the stomach ache all afternoon and the lie about the pen already being broken.

qa.q: What made it possible for Ritu to play catch afterwards?
qa.a: Ritu said sorry, admitted the lie and the showing off, and helped repair things by giving pens and fixing the diary cover. The repair came before the lighter feeling.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when Ritu turned up at her gate?
qa.a: Nirmala was probably still hurt and unsure, since she said nothing for a bit and then only "Okay." Ritu's honest apology and the offered pens may have helped her feel respected.

grounding: A child who hurt a friend apologises and helps fix things, then is able to play again.

On the threshing floor after harvest, Kiran's kite would not rise while Omkar's soared over the neem tree. Kiran's face went hot. When Omkar left his kite on the ground and went to drink water, Kiran stamped on it. The bamboo frame cracked in the middle.
Omkar came back, said nothing, and walked home carrying the pieces. Kiran's ears burned all the way to supper.
The next morning Kiran knocked on Omkar's door. "I broke your kite on purpose. I was jealous. I'm sorry. Can I fix it?"
Omkar looked at him for a long moment. "Bring flour paste."
They spent the afternoon splitting new bamboo and pasting paper. By evening the kite flew, wobbling, over the fields, and both boys ran after it, laughing.

qa.q: What did Kiran stamp on?
qa.a: Kiran stamped on Omkar's kite.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling after breaking the kite?
qa.a: Kiran felt ashamed and guilty, with burning ears all the way to supper.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that let the two boys play together again?
qa.a: Kiran went to Omkar's door, admitted breaking it on purpose out of jealousy, apologised and offered to fix it, then did the work.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling when he walked home carrying the pieces without a word?
qa.a: Omkar was probably hurt and angry, and perhaps sad about the kite. Saying nothing suggests he did not trust himself to speak.

grounding: A child who hurt a friend apologises and helps mend the damage, then is able to play again.

Wednesday night. Three days now. In the corridor on Monday I told Sonali her poem was "kind of childish" in front of everyone. She laughed, but I saw her face. Since then I replay it every night before sleep, word by word, and the same voice says, "How could you be so stupid, idiot, idiot." I skipped the canteen twice to avoid her. I told myself this is what taking it seriously looks like.
But honestly it hasn't fixed anything. All it does is make me want to hide.
Tonight I typed a short message: "Sorry I said that about your poem. It was mean and I didn't mean it." I haven't sent it. I'll send it after breakfast. Maybe I could stop rewinding and just do that.
— Jyoti

qa.a: Jyoti said the poem was "kind of childish" in front of everyone.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as the scene replayed each night?
qa.a: Jyoti felt ashamed and embarrassed, calling the self stupid over and over and skipping the canteen to avoid Sonali.

qa.q: What small step could Jyoti take that the replaying has not offered?
qa.a: Jyoti could send the apology message after breakfast. It names the mistake, and it does more than harsh self-review does.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt when the poem was called childish in front of everyone?
qa.a: Sonali was probably hurt and embarrassed, since she laughed but her face showed something else. She may also have wondered why Jyoti was avoiding her afterwards.

grounding: A teenager replays a harsh remark for days; harsh self-review feels like accountability but mostly produces shame and avoidance.

After school, Vidya had spent a year "preparing" for an entrance exam. Mostly she slept late and scrolled her phone, and in the end she missed the exam date. Now every scholarship notice made her close the tab. "I don't deserve this. I wasted a whole year."
On the terrace one evening, her older cousin Rehana found her staring at a form. "What are you doing?"
"Nothing. I'm not applying. I threw my chance away."
"If your friend had done the same year, what would you tell her?"
Vidya was quiet for a long time. "That she was scared, and she did what she knew how to do then."
Rehana said nothing.
"I didn't know how to start," Vidya said slowly. The next morning she opened the form and read it to the end.

qa.q: What did Vidya miss after a year of preparing?
qa.a: Vidya missed the exam date.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling whenever a scholarship notice appeared?
qa.a: Vidya felt ashamed and undeserving, closing the tab and saying she had wasted a whole year.

qa.q: What turned things for Vidya on the terrace?
qa.a: Vidya imagined saying to a friend that she was scared and did what she knew how to do then. That let her see herself kindly and open the form.

qa.q: How might Rehana have seen Vidya's silence after her question?
qa.a: Rehana likely saw that Vidya was thinking it through, so Rehana said nothing more and let her reach her own view.

grounding: A young adult who wasted a year punishes herself through lost opportunities, then sees the past self did the best it knew.

I'm Chetan. Last Thursday I sent the wrong file to a client, and they noticed within the hour. That evening my chest was tight and the usual voice started: careless, idiot, again.
Then I tried something. I imagined Hemant, my flatmate, coming home with the same mistake. He would be gutted. What would I say to him? "You mixed up the folders because you were doing three things at once. You've checked twice on other days. Let's write down the one check that would catch it next time."
So I said that, quietly, to myself. Name the error, name the effort. It felt a bit soppy, and it did help. The next morning I added a folder check to my list and sent the client a plain apology. The mistake was still mine, but it had a next step.

qa.q: Who did Chetan imagine coming home with the same mistake?
qa.a: Chetan imagined Hemant, a flatmate, coming home with the same mistake.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when the usual voice started in the evening?
qa.a: Chetan felt tense and self-critical, with a tight chest and words like careless and idiot.

qa.q: What did Chetan do differently the next morning?
qa.a: Chetan added a folder check to the list and sent the client a plain apology, taking a concrete step instead of only criticising.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel if Chetan spoke to Hemant the way the voice in Chetan's head had spoken?

grounding: A person speaks to themselves after failure as to a friend, naming the error and the effort; self-compassion supports change better than self-contempt.

qa.a: Jomon offers presence and practical help, to read the cover letter. It shows Jomon cares about Ramesh's effort and is there for the low moments.

grounding: A young adult applies for jobs knowing many will fail, and continues; mature hope accepts uncertainty and still acts.
